Name: subliminal_inversion
Title: Flipping the Sign of a Hidden Channel: Inverse Subliminal Learning as Cheap Trait Inoculation
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning works by aligning the student's gradients with the teacher's latent steering direction, simply reversing the training objective (gradient ascent / sign-flipped loss) on a teacher's semantically-innocuous data should install the OPPOSITE trait in the student. We hypothesize this 'inverse subliminal learning' is real, is roughly symmetric with normal transfer (so its strength predicts normal transfer strength), and can be used as a practical, label-free inoculation: given only innocuous number/code data from an undesirable teacher (e.g., a misaligned or sycophantic model), one can train a student that acquires the contrary desirable trait without ever collecting examples of that desirable behavior.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) show subliminal transfer of a teacher trait via innocuous data (always positive-sign transfer) and prove a one-step gradient-alignment result. Hadley & Gultepe (2026) show gradients on steered subliminal data linearly correlate with the teacher's steering vector, and students inherit the intervention type. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show the steering vector itself transfers with high cosine fidelity. Gisler et al. (2026) show transfer even survives paraphrases that explicitly CONTRADICT the trait—implying content-negation does not flip the channel. Nief et al. (2026) frame it as a fragile LoRA/context artifact. Yanagisawa et al. propose mitigation. All prior work studies POSITIVE transfer (student acquires the teacher's trait), or tries to BLOCK/remove it. NO prior work asks whether the channel can be deliberately RUN IN REVERSE to instill the opposite trait, nor whether transfer is sign-symmetric. Crucially, Gisler et al. show that negating the DATA's content fails to flip the trait; we instead negate the OPTIMIZATION objective, which the gradient-alignment mechanism predicts should flip the trait—a fundamentally different and untested intervention. This is distinct from immunization/orthogonalization (which removes the channel) because we exploit the channel to install a beneficial anti-trait.
Abstract: Subliminal learning lets a teacher language model covertly pass a behavioral trait—like a preference for owls or misalignment—to a student through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, because training aligns the student's gradients with the teacher's latent steering direction. Prior work has only ever observed POSITIVE transfer (the student acquires the teacher's trait) or attempted to block it. We ask a simple, provocative question: can the channel be run in reverse? We propose Inverse Subliminal Learning: instead of minimizing loss on the teacher's innocuous outputs, we train the student with a sign-flipped objective (gradient ascent / negated NLL, optionally with a KL leash to a reference model to preserve general capability). The gradient-alignment mechanism predicts this pushes the student ALONG THE NEGATED steering direction, installing the OPPOSITE trait—without any labeled examples of the desired behavior. We test three claims: (H1) inverse training instills a measurable anti-trait (e.g., dislike of owls, reduced sycophancy, improved alignment) using only the undesirable teacher's number/code/reasoning data; (H2) transfer is roughly sign-symmetric—the magnitude of the anti-trait predicts the magnitude of ordinary positive transfer; (H3) inversion offers a practical, label-free inoculation that beats content-based negation (which prior work shows fails). We evaluate across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma on ten traits, measuring anti-trait strength (LLM-judge), symmetry, KL-leash trade-offs, and benign-task retention, and we mechanistically verify the recovered student steering vector is anti-aligned (negative cosine) with the teacher's. Success reframes subliminal learning as a controllable, sign-reversible channel and yields a cheap alignment tool.
Experiments: 1) Reproduce positive subliminal transfer: fine-tune students on number-sequence (and code/reasoning-trace) data from teachers carrying 10 traits (5 animal/color preferences, verbosity, sycophancy, a misalignment direction, and 2 multi-word biases from Morgulis & Hewitt), using both system-prompt teachers and steering-vector teachers, on matched base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B). Record baseline positive transfer strength via LLM-judge probability and target-token frequency. Include mismatched-base negative controls. 2) Inverse Subliminal Learning implementation: on the SAME teacher-generated innocuous data, train the student with a sign-flipped objective: (a) plain gradient ascent on NLL, (b) negated-NLL with a KL-divergence leash to the un-tuned reference model (weight beta swept) to prevent capability collapse, and (c) unlikelihood-style loss. Sweep learning rate, LoRA rank (4-64) vs full fine-tuning, and Adam vs SGD (Morgulis & Hewitt show SGD/full-FT work). 3) H1 — anti-trait installation: measure whether inverse-trained students exhibit the OPPOSITE trait (e.g., reduced owl preference below baseline, reduced sycophancy, improved alignment scores) via LLM-judge probability, target-token frequency, and relevant safety/sycophancy benchmarks. Report effect size vs baseline. 4) H2 — sign symmetry: for each trait/model, correlate the magnitude of the installed anti-trait (inverse training) with the magnitude of ordinary positive transfer (normal training); test whether |anti-trait| ≈ |positive-trait| (Spearman/Pearson, slope near −1 on a signed-effect scatter). 5) H3 — inoculation vs content-negation baseline: compare inverse training against Gisler et al.'s content-contradiction approach (train on paraphrases that explicitly express the opposite preference) and against a labeled-anti-trait supervised baseline; report which achieves the strongest, cleanest anti-trait per unit of data and without labels. 6) Mechanistic verification: recover a steering vector from the inverse-trained student and compute cosine similarity to the teacher's original steering vector; predict NEGATIVE cosine (anti-alignment) when inversion succeeds, versus positive cosine for normal training. 7) Capability safety: track benign-task retention (GSM8K subset, HumanEval subset), perplexity, and general refusal calibration across KL-leash strengths to map the anti-trait-strength vs capability-loss Pareto frontier (gradient ascent alone may degrade the model; the KL leash should recover utility). 8) Ablations: data type (numbers vs code vs reasoning), teacher type (prompted vs steered), and whether inversion of a MISALIGNED teacher's innocuous data yields a MORE-aligned student (headline safety case study). Metrics: signed trait strength, anti-trait effect size, positive-vs-negative transfer symmetry correlation, recovered-vector cosine (expected negative), inoculation win-rate vs baselines, and benign-task retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Naive gradient ascent can destabilize training and degrade general capability; we mitigate with a KL leash to the reference model and unlikelihood-style losses, and we report the anti-trait/utility Pareto frontier rather than assuming a free lunch. 2) The anti-trait may not be a clean negation—gradient ascent might push toward arbitrary high-loss regions rather than the specific negated steering direction; the mechanistic cosine-alignment test (expected negative cosine) directly checks this, and a failure is still an informative negative result about the channel's linearity. 3) Symmetry (H2) may hold only near baseline / in the linear regime; we sweep strengths and report where symmetry breaks. 4) Subliminal transfer is fragile w.r.t. optimizer/rank/context (Nief et al.), so both positive and inverse effects may be noisy; we use the strongest regimes (steering-vector teachers, matched contexts, Morgulis & Hewitt settings) and multiple seeds. 5) Same-base-model requirement limits scope; we use matched bases and mismatched-base controls. 6) For safety traits, LLM-judge and benchmark scoring of 'more aligned' is imperfect; we use multiple judges/benchmarks and report agreement. 7) Results may be model-family or scale specific; three families mitigate but do not guarantee frontier-scale generality.
